The lighthouse keeper wrote in the log every evening, and the log was kept in a drawer beneath the lamp. On calm nights the entries were short. The sea was quiet, the wind was from the west, and the ships passed far out beyond the reef. On rough nights the entries were longer, and the keeper wrote them slowly, because the lamp swayed and the ink ran.

In the spring a letter came from the harbour office. The office wished to know how many ships had passed in the winter, and how many had signalled to the shore. The keeper read the letter twice and went down to the drawer. He counted the ships in the log, one page at a time, and wrote the numbers on a sheet of paper.

There were forty ships in the winter. Eleven had signalled to the shore, and two had asked for a pilot. The keeper wrote the numbers in a clear hand and sealed the letter with wax. Then he walked down to the village, where the post was collected on Tuesday and Friday.

The woman at the post office weighed the letter and put it in the bag. She asked about the winter, and the keeper told her about the storm in February, when the waves had reached the lower window. She said that the village had heard the bell all night. He said that the bell had rung by itself, because the wind had been so strong.

On the way back the keeper stopped at the bakery and bought bread for the week. The road along the cliff was dry, and the sea below was the colour of slate. At the top of the hill he turned and looked at the village, at the boats drawn up on the shingle and the smoke rising from the chimneys. Then he went on to the lighthouse, climbed the stairs, and lit the lamp for the night.

The next morning the keeper cleaned the lens and trimmed the wick. He wrote in the log that the night had been calm, that the wind was from the north, and that one ship had passed close to the reef before dawn. He did not know the name of the ship. He wrote only that its lights had been green and white, and that it had turned away from the rocks in good time.
